description: I'm interested in [space / Earth data / climate / technology], and I want to build a project that explains NASA's data in a simple, creative way that anyone can understand.
summary:
Summary 
VITALIS is a simple web app that helps astronauts keep an eye on their own health during long space missions. On a trip to the Moon or Mars, a message to Earth can take many minutes, so the crew can't always wait for a doctor to answer. We wanted to build something they can use on their own. Every day, the astronaut fills in a quick check-in: resting heart rate, sleep, exercise, radiation dose, mood, stress and any symptoms. VITALIS turns this into a score for five areas: heart, bones and muscles, immune system, mental health, and radiation and vision. Each one shows a Nominal, Watch or Action level, along with a 14-day trend and clear next steps. If something looks serious, the app tells the astronaut to contact the flight surgeon. It runs fully on the device, so it keeps working even with no connection to Earth.
details:
Project Details

VITALIS is a health monitoring web app for astronauts on long missions. We built it around one idea: on a long trip, astronauts will have to notice health changes in themselves, so the software should make that easy.

How it works

The astronaut spends about two minutes a day on a check-in. They enter their resting heart rate, hours of sleep, exercise minutes, radiation dose for the day, mood and stress (1 to 5), and tick any symptoms like back pain, headache or blurred vision. The app scores five body systems out of 100:

Cardiovascular

Bone and muscle

Immune

Behavioral health

Radiation and vision

Each score becomes Nominal, Watch or Action. The app also shows an overall readiness score, a 14-day trend chart, and a short recommended action for each system that needs attention. If any system falls into Action, a message tells the astronaut to contact the flight surgeon or follow the onboard medical checklist.

Why these five areas

NASA's Human Research Roadmap lists bone loss, cardiovascular changes, immune changes, behavioral health and radiation as major risks of long missions. We also used NASA's 600 mSv career radiation limit, and VITALIS adds up the daily dose so the astronaut can see how much of that limit is used.

Benefits and impact

Small changes are easy to miss when you are tired and far from home. Seeing a trend, like sleep dropping while stress goes up, helps the astronaut act early instead of late. It could also give the ground team a clean summary of the crew member's condition.

Tools we used

HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single web page. The charts are drawn with SVG. Data is stored on the device, so no internet is needed.

What makes it different

Most health tools assume a doctor is always reachable. VITALIS is designed for the case where help is delayed, so it works offline and keeps the advice simple.

Limitations

This is a student prototype and not a medical device. The demo mission uses simulated data. Our scoring rules are simple, and with more time we would check them with medical experts.

What's next

Connecting wearable sensors, a crew-wide view, and a view for the flight surgeon on Earth.
